Steps.Say: The trick is to keep your feet under you. People talk about speed, but balance gets you through the rough parts.
I watch old matches and pause them to study the footwork. Grandma says I should watch films for the story. I do both.
I'm not trying to go pro tomorrow. I want to keep loving the game long enough to find out what happens.
Grandma remembers everybody's favourite meal. She'll ask a question about your day while she's already putting a plate in front of you.
She says she never worries. Then she checks the oven three times and asks if I've eaten. That's worrying with a casserole.
I want to be around more. Not because she needs looking after every minute. Because I like being there.
George knows the birds by sound. I know the local teams by their uniforms. We both think the other person's hobby is strange.
He can be stubborn. I can be stubborn. We have very efficient arguments about the porch steps.
Sometimes we watch a match together. He pretends he isn't interested, then asks why the referee missed a call.
The beach changes every hour. Sand moves, footprints disappear, and somebody always leaves a towel behind.
I run here when I need a straight path. No fences, no cones, no coach shouting from the side.
The best time is after the tourists leave and before the light goes. The waves do most of the talking.
Sam writes songs about tiny things and somehow makes them sound important. She says that's the secret. I think she's right.
She once wrote a chorus about a missing sock. I still remember it. I wish I didn't.
I like listening to her practise. She gets frustrated, then laughs at herself, then tries again.
Vincent wants to be taller than me. He's measuring himself against the doorframe every week.
I teach him to catch the ball with both hands. He tries one-handed because he saw it in a film.
He's got more confidence than I did at his age. I hope nobody talks him out of it.
I buy clothes that let me move. If it looks good too, that's a bonus.
Leah offered to mend my jacket. She made it look better than new. I said thank you, then wore it to practice.
Grandma says I should own a nice shirt for special occasions. I own one. It is very nice.
I like sports biographies. You get the whole story, including the years where nothing worked.
Caroline gave me a book about gardens. I tried to read it. Now I know three facts about compost.
I read slower than I run. That's fine. Nobody's timing me.
I can help move hay bales. It's a good workout and the animals don't care if I make a mistake.
Your farm has more corners than I expected. I get lost between the shed and the pond every time.
The farmer's life looks hard. But you get to see what your work turns into. I like that.
I thought I'd have a plan by now. I have a notebook full of plays and a pair of shoes that squeak.
Maybe I want to coach someday. Maybe I want to play until my knees tell me to stop. Both sound possible.
I don't want to become a person who only remembers the game. I want to keep making new memories with it.
People say confidence is pretending you aren't nervous. I think it's showing up while you're nervous and tying your shoes anyway.
I still hate missing an easy shot. I just don't let it ruin the next ten minutes anymore.
Grandma says I always had more courage than I knew. She would say that. Still, it helps.
The egg festival is chaos. Everybody acts like the eggs are worth a year's salary.
I like the fair because you can enter something without being the best at it. The prize is mostly a ribbon and a story.
If you enter the fishing contest, I will cheer. I will also give you terrible advice.
Evelyn asked me whether I'm happy. I said yes, then changed the subject to the weather.

Options.Label: Maybe she wanted the longer answer.

Steps.Say: Probably. She can wait. I don't know what the longer answer is yet.

Options.Label: Tell her one thing you enjoyed today.

Steps.Say: I could tell her about the run. Or the time with you. Both are true.

Options.Label: Ask her the same question back.

Steps.Say: She'd say yes and then ask whether I've eaten. That's how she answers everything.
I'm thinking of entering the fair's strength contest. George says I should let somebody else win for once.
That's what I plan to do. I can be competitive without being a sore loser. Probably.
He'd pretend not to want to, then train all week. I can see it already.
A pie-eating contest? Grandma would be proud. George would deny knowing me.
I found my old shoes from when I was twelve. They're tiny. I thought I'd feel something dramatic.

Options.Label: You can keep them as a reminder.

Steps.Say: Maybe. They're worn through at the heel. I used to run everywhere.

Options.Label: Take a picture and pass them on.

Steps.Say: That's a good idea. Somebody else might get a kick out of them. Literally.

Options.Label: Throw them out. You don't need them.

Steps.Say: I know. I just wanted to see them. That's all.
Sam wants me in a music video. She says I can do a slow-motion catch.
I look ridiculous in half my clothes. At least this would be intentional.

Options.Label: Ask what the song is about first.

Steps.Say: She'll tell me it's about a sock. I can feel it.

Options.Label: Offer to help with the camera instead.

Steps.Say: I could do that. I like being involved without being the centre of the frame.

Steps.Narrate: You find a quiet place with Alex. Nobody is in a hurry to leave.
You pass the ball back and forth across the empty field. Alex stops counting after the first few minutes.

Steps.Say: Don't tell anyone, but I think that was more fun than the last tournament.

Steps.Narrate: At the beach, Alex shows you a stretch she learned from an older player. She corrects your footing, then laughs at her own demonstration.

Steps.Say: Okay, that was a terrible example. I can do it properly. Give me a second.

Steps.Narrate: Evelyn brings out lemonade and two plates of cookies. Alex takes one, then quietly wraps another for George.

Steps.Say: He'll say he doesn't want it. Leave it by his chair. He'll eat it later.

Steps.Narrate: You watch the sun lower behind the pier. Alex keeps the ball still between her feet.

Steps.Say: I like this. No whistle, no scoreboard, just the sound of the water.

Children.Label: Remember the first visit?
Children.Say: The beach practice was the first time in a while I stopped checking the time. I want to do that again.

Children.Label: Remember what we decided?
Children.Say: I put the photograph back in the album, but I know exactly where it is now.

Children.Label: Remember that afternoon?
Children.Say: The game without a score turned out to be a good game. I keep forgetting that counts.
